cards.front: Cultural safety differs from cultural awareness in that it is defined by the [___], not by the clinician's intent.
cards.context:
Cultural safety is judged by the patient, not asserted by the clinician — the test is whether the family experienced the encounter as safe, not whether you intended it to be.

That is what distinguishes it from cultural awareness, which is only knowing that difference exists.

cards.front: Paediatric bones: thicker periosteum (faster healing), [___] is weak point (fractures more common than dislocations), more porous (bend before break).
cards.context:
Three differences from adult bone: (1) thick periosteum acts as an internal splint — faster healing, less displacement.

(2) the open physis (growth plate) is the weakest link, so it fails before the joint, making fractures commoner than dislocations; (3) more porous bone bends or buckles before it snaps (greenstick, torus).

cards.front: [___] abuse affects roughly 1 in 3 Australian children (ACMS), yet is among the least likely to be reported or identified.
cards.context:
It is under-reported precisely because it leaves no bruise or fracture — there is no objective injury to trigger a notification, so it slips past clinicians and teachers who are watching for physical signs.

Look for behavioural indicators instead: withdrawal, excessive compliance, age-inappropriate behaviour, self-harm, and fear of caregivers. ACMS prevalence is around 30%.

cards.front: A positive HBsAg (a surface antigen) means current Hepatitis B infection, whereas a positive [___] (a surface antibody) means immunity from vaccination or cleared infection.
cards.context:
Read the three Hep B markers as a story, not a list. 'B surface ANTIGEN' is a piece of the virus itself, so finding it means the virus is currently in the body (current infection).

'Surface ANTIBODY' (anti-HBs) is the body's protective response — present after vaccination or after clearing the infection, so it means immunity.

The third marker, anti-HBc (core antibody), means the person has at some point been exposed to the real virus — it is positive in current and past natural infection, but NOT after vaccination.

cards.front: Imaging clue for the toddler abdominal mass: [___] within a mass that crosses the midline favours neuroblastoma; Wilms' tumour rarely shows it.
cards.context:
The neural-crest tumour outgrows its blood supply and necroses, and necrotic tumour mineralises — visible on CT in most cases. Wilms', a renal-parenchyma tumour, only rarely mineralises.

The company each mass keeps differs too: neuroblastoma children are often unwell (fevers, weight loss, limp from marrow spread; median ~18 months), while Wilms' children are classically well (peak 3-4 years).

cards.front: An isolated raised ALP in a well, growing child is bone rather than liver — the give-away is that the biliary enzyme [___] stays normal, whereas in cholestasis the two rise together.
cards.context:
The discriminator between bone ALP and biliary ALP is the enzyme beside it. Gamma-glutamyl transferase comes from biliary epithelium and not from bone.

So the two rise TOGETHER in cholestasis, and ALP rises ALONE in growth, rickets and healing fractures. An isolated ALP with a normal GGT in a well, growing child needs no liver work-up.

Transient benign hyperphosphatasaemia of infancy is worth knowing as the extreme version: a well toddler with an ALP in the thousands, a normal GGT, and spontaneous resolution over weeks.

cards.front: Most common cause of paediatric gastroenteritis was rotavirus (now reduced by vaccination); [___] now predominates; bacterial causes are minority.
cards.context:
Acute gastroenteritis is the commonest cause of vomiting + diarrhoea in children. Rotavirus dominated before universal vaccination; norovirus now leads.

Bacterial causes (Salmonella, Campylobacter, Shigella, ETEC) account for ~5-10%.

cards.front: Gillick competence allows a minor to consent to medical treatment if they have sufficient understanding and intelligence; confidentiality has limits (harm to self/others, mandatory [___]).
cards.context:
Gillick competence (UK case law, adopted internationally) lets a minor under 16 consent if they have sufficient understanding to comprehend the proposal — risks, benefits, alternatives.

Confidentiality limits: harm to self/others, mandatory reporting, notifiable diseases.

reference.title: Engaging with and assessing the adolescent patient

cards.front: A pregnant woman exposed to varicella with unknown immunity should first have her [___] checked to confirm she is susceptible.
cards.context: Many adults are already immune from past infection, so confirm susceptibility before giving immunoglobulin. A non-immune pregnant woman is at risk of severe varicella pneumonia.

cards.front: In Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, Group A Streptococcus preceding acute rheumatic fever is often [___]-borne rather than from pharyngitis.
cards.context:
The classic 'strep throat then rheumatic fever' story under-describes the Australian pattern, where skin sores are a major reservoir.

Treat pyoderma and scabies seriously — they are part of the ARF prevention pathway, not a cosmetic problem. Scabies drives the skin sores, which drive the strep, which drives the ARF.

cards.front: A continuous 'machinery' murmur with bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure indicates [___].
cards.context:
PDA is the only common left-to-right shunt that flows continuously — aortic pressure exceeds pulmonary pressure throughout systole and diastole, producing the machinery murmur loudest at the left infraclavicular area.

Bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure come from diastolic run-off into the pulmonary circulation.

cards.front: Congenital dermal melanocytosis (the Mongolian spot) is classically found over the [___] region.
cards.context:
Congenital dermal melanocytosis — the Mongolian spot — is a benign blue-black macule, usually single, most often over the lumbosacral region and then the back, present at birth and fading during childhood.

It is most common in babies of Asian, African and Hispanic ancestry. It is dermal melanin seen through the skin, not a bruise: it does not change colour over days and it is not tender.

cards.front: Compared with a low-risk setting, the Jones diagnostic threshold for acute rheumatic fever in a high-incidence population is [___].
cards.context: High-risk Jones criteria use broader joint manifestations and lower fever and inflammatory-marker cut-offs. A presentation below low-risk cut-offs may therefore still meet criteria.

cards.front: IV/IO adrenaline in paediatric arrest is [___] mL/kg of the 1:10,000 (100 microg/mL) preparation.
cards.context:
1:10,000 means 1 g in 10,000 mL — 100 microg/mL. So the 10 microg/kg arrest dose converts to 0.1 mL/kg, and the pre-filled 10 mL minijet holds 1 mg: the whole syringe is the adult dose.

Doing this conversion is the doctor's job, done BEFORE speaking. The nurse drawing up should never be handed weight arithmetic mid-arrest.

The trap option in exams is '0.1 mL/kg of 1:1000 IV' — familiar numbers, wrong strength, a 10-fold overdose.

cards.front: A partial bronchial obstruction that admits air on inspiration but blocks it on expiration causes air trapping, known as obstructive [___].
cards.context:
The mechanism has a name that is worth carrying, because it explains why the lung cannot deflate.

A ball-valve obstruction admits air on inspiration and blocks its escape on expiration. Complete obstruction does the opposite — the distal lung collapses.

cards.front: SCID = severe combined immunodeficiency; presents with opportunistic infections + FTT; absent thymus on CXR; stem cell transplant before [___] months gives best outcomes.
cards.context:
Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) is the most severe primary immunodeficiency — defective T-cell development with variable B-cell involvement. Lab signature: lymphopenia (especially T cells), absent thymus on CXR.

Without treatment, infants present with opportunistic infections (PJP, CMV, fungi) and FTT in first months.

Early diagnosis and infection prevention improve transplant survival. Transplant by 3.5 months is associated with high survival; older infection-free infants can also do well.

cards.front: The Centor feature that argues for group A strep rather than a viral sore throat is absence of [___].
cards.context: Fever, tonsillar exudate and tender anterior nodes can occur in viral illness too. The Centor discriminator that argues against a simple viral URI is the absence of cough.

cards.front: In CF, the nebulised mucolytic [___] cleaves extracellular DNA released from neutrophils, reducing mucus viscosity.
cards.context:
Dornase alfa is recombinant human DNase I — it digests the extracellular DNA released by dead neutrophils, which is the dominant viscosity contributor in CF mucus.

The result is thinner mucus that clears with physiotherapy. Effect builds over weeks of daily use.

cards.front: Heart rate also falls with age: about [___] bpm in a term newborn, settling to roughly 60-115 bpm by mid-adolescence.
cards.context:
A small child's stroke volume is fixed and small, so cardiac output is almost entirely rate-dependent. That is why the resting rate starts high and why a bradycardic child is peri-arrest rather than merely fit.

The adult range is not reached until mid-adolescence, so a heart rate of 140 means very different things in a toddler and in a fourteen-year-old.

cards.front: Reticulocytes index marrow output: a high count points to blood loss or haemolysis (cells made fine but destroyed), whereas a low count points to a marrow [___] problem.
cards.context:
Reticulocytes are immature red cells just released from marrow, so their count is a live readout of marrow output. This is the single best bedside split of the anaemia differential.

High count = marrow is working, so red cells are being lost or destroyed faster than made (bleeding, haemolysis). Low/normal count = the marrow itself is the bottleneck (deficiency, suppression, infiltration).

cards.front: An overweight 10-14 year old has hip pain, a limp, and the leg held externally rotated. The diagnosis is [___].
cards.context: This presentation is slipped capital femoral epiphysis. Knee pain can be referred from the hip, so examine the hip.

cards.front: Initial medical management of Budd-Chiari syndrome is [___], alongside treating the underlying cause.
cards.context:
First-line medical treatment, started as soon as the diagnosis is made, and usually lifelong because the underlying prothrombotic tendency does not go away.

It does not clear the existing obstruction by itself — that is what the interventional rungs are for — but it stops the clot extending while the cause is investigated.

cards.front: Positive stool [___] indicate carbohydrate malabsorption, such as lactose intolerance or mucosal disease.
cards.context:
Unabsorbed sugar reaching the colon stays sugar — a positive stool test for reducing substances points to carbohydrate malabsorption (e.g. lactose intolerance, or mucosal disease like coeliac).

It complements the stool osmotic gap, which is also raised in osmotic (carbohydrate) diarrhoea.

cards.front: Foreign body aspiration peaks at age [___] years; the right main bronchus is more commonly affected.
cards.context:
Right main bronchus is wider, more vertical, and almost a direct continuation of the trachea — gravity favours objects entering it. The 1-3 year peak reflects oral exploration combined with poor chewing.

Common objects: peanuts (most common organic), grapes, small toys. Round smooth objects can lodge at the larynx.

cards.front: Faltering [___] is a central complication of chronic liver disease in children and should be tracked at every visit.
cards.context:
Chronic liver disease is a growth disease in paediatrics. The liver handles protein synthesis, energy metabolism, and bile-dependent fat absorption — all impaired as disease progresses.

Faltering growth is often the metric parents notice first, and it predicts outcome independently of the liver biochemistry. Every clinic visit should plot height and weight on age-appropriate charts.

cards.front: After significant chickenpox exposure, a healthy susceptible child receives varicella vaccine; a susceptible child on chemotherapy receives [___] instead.
cards.context:
A healthy susceptible contact can receive live varicella vaccine after exposure.

Chemotherapy makes that vaccine unsafe, so the susceptible immunocompromised contact receives passive varicella-zoster immunoglobulin instead.

cards.front: Single-dose oral ondansetron (0.15 mg/kg wafer) reduces vomiting in paediatric gastroenteritis and the need for [___] fluids; give before attempting oral rehydration.
cards.context:
Single-dose ondansetron wafer (0.15 mg/kg, max 8 mg) halves persistent vomiting in mild-to-moderate paediatric gastroenteritis and reduces the need for IV fluids and admission (Cochrane evidence is strong).

Practical: give the wafer first, wait 15-20 minutes, then start oral rehydration with small frequent volumes. Avoid in infants <6 months and known long QT syndrome; one dose is usually enough.

cards.front: Pleural air between the mediastinum and lung gives an unusually crisp mediastinal outline on a neonatal film — the etched [___] border sign.
cards.context:
Neonatal pneumothorax does not look like the adult version, and this named sign is why it gets missed.

Pleural air interposed between the mediastinum and lung outlines the mediastinal border unusually crisply. Recognising an over-sharp cardiac border on a sick ventilated neonate is often the only clue.

cards.front: On a child's LFTs, a rise in the hepatocellular enzymes ALT and [___] points to liver-cell damage, rather than blocked bile flow.
cards.context:
ALT and AST live inside hepatocytes and leak out when liver cells are injured (e.g. viral hepatitis, paracetamol overdose). A hepatocellular picture is enzyme-leak from damaged cells.

ALT is the more liver-specific of the two; AST also rises with muscle injury, so isolated AST is not always the liver.

cards.front: A stable child has pancytopenia and hepatosplenomegaly, without airway compromise. Before corticosteroids, the haematologist obtains a [___] aspirate to establish the diagnosis.
cards.context:
Pancytopenia and organomegaly warrant investigation for marrow infiltration. Marrow sampling establishes blast morphology and enables immunophenotyping.

When clinically safe, collect diagnostic samples before steroids because steroids can reduce blasts. Stabilisation and urgent haematology discussion come first; life-threatening complications may alter this sequence.

cards.front: DSM-5 autism requires social-communication deficits plus [___], repetitive behaviours, both present from early childhood.
cards.context: DSM-5 autism is two domains, not one. Social-communication problems without restricted repetitive behaviours is not autism, and the reverse is not either.

cards.front: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a defective [___] chloride channel.
cards.context: One faulty channel explains the whole disease. Defective CFTR can't move chloride (and water) onto epithelial surfaces, so secretions everywhere — lungs, pancreas, gut, sweat ducts — become thick and dehydrated.

cards.front: A cyanotic infant becomes deeply blue and distressed while feeding. The immediate position that raises systemic resistance is [___].
cards.context:
Knee-to-chest positioning raises systemic vascular resistance and reduces right-to-left shunting during a hypercyanotic spell.

Give oxygen and urgent clinical support as part of the same emergency response.

reference.title: Cyanotic episodes in congenital heart disease

cards.front: A 2-year-old suddenly coughs while eating peanuts, then has persistent unilateral wheeze and one lung remains hyperinflated on expiration. The definitive diagnostic and therapeutic procedure is [___].
cards.context: Sudden choking, unilateral wheeze, and expiratory air trapping identify an inhaled bronchial foreign body even if the inspiratory film is normal. Rigid bronchoscopy both confirms the diagnosis and removes it.

cards.front: At the routine 6-month NIP visit a healthy non-Indigenous infant receives only the [___] DTPa-hepB-IPV-Hib vaccine.
cards.context:
The 6-month visit is the one people pad. For a healthy non-Indigenous infant the NIP gives only the hexavalent DTPa-hepB-IPV-Hib.

Pneumococcal conjugate at this age is an extra dose for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and for children with specified medical-risk conditions — not a routine extra in 'some states'.

cards.front: A well child with chronic hearing loss, an intact eardrum, normal canal volume and a flat tympanogram likely has glue ear; a type C trace instead indicates [___] middle-ear pressure.
cards.context:
A flat trace with normal ear-canal volume and an intact drum supports middle-ear effusion.

A large canal volume suggests a perforation or patent grommet; a small volume suggests canal or probe blockage.

Type C indicates negative middle-ear pressure, commonly from Eustachian-tube dysfunction.

cards.front: Primary haemostasis (platelet plug, mucocutaneous bleeding) is mediated by platelets and vWF; secondary haemostasis (deep bleeding) is mediated by [___].
cards.context:
Primary haemostasis: platelets + vWF form the initial platelet plug at sites of vascular injury.

Secondary haemostasis: coagulation factor cascade generates fibrin thrombus stabilising the clot.

Defects cause deep bleeding (joints, muscles, post-surgical) — haemophilia A/B, factor deficiencies, anticoagulation.

cards.front: The five CRASH features of Kawasaki disease are [___], rash, adenopathy, strawberry tongue and hand and foot changes.
cards.context:
CRASH is the retrieval handle: Conjunctivitis, Rash, Adenopathy, Strawberry tongue, Hands and feet. Fever is required on top of these, not one of them.

The features accumulate rather than appearing together, so a child seen early can look incomplete and still have the disease.

Conjunctivitis is bilateral and non-purulent, and the node qualifies at 1.5 cm or more, usually on one side.

cards.front: Reticulocytes index marrow output: a high count points to blood loss or [___] (cells made fine but destroyed), whereas a low count points to a marrow production problem.
cards.context:
Reticulocytes are immature red cells just released from marrow, so their count is a live readout of marrow output. This is the single best bedside split of the anaemia differential.

High count = marrow is working, so red cells are being lost or destroyed faster than made (bleeding, haemolysis). Low/normal count = the marrow itself is the bottleneck (deficiency, suppression, infiltration).

cards.front: The commonest cause of childhood nephrotic syndrome, usually steroid-responsive, is [___] disease.
cards.context: In children, nephrotic syndrome is usually minimal change disease — so typical cases (1–10y, no atypical features) are treated with steroids empirically WITHOUT a biopsy, and most respond.

cards.front: A child with unexplained developmental delay is tested for small deletions or duplications of chromosomal material using a [___].
cards.context:
This test looks for gains or losses of DNA across the genome, at a finer resolution than a conventional karyotype.

A detected change needs clinical interpretation: some results remain of uncertain significance. Finding a variant does not automatically explain the developmental difficulty.

cards.front: Haemophilia is inherited and X-linked, so it almost always affects [___], often with a family history. ITP is acquired after a viral illness and affects either sex.
cards.context:
Who gets it, and after what, splits the two diagnoses. ITP is acquired — it follows a viral illness in a previously well child, so it can affect any child of either sex with no family history.

Haemophilia is inherited and X-linked recessive.

Because boys have only one X chromosome, an affected gene is not masked, so haemophilia almost always presents in boys, often with a maternal-side family history of bleeding.

cards.front: Bronchiolitis management is [___] (oxygen/hydration); bronchodilators are NOT routinely recommended because obstruction is mechanical, not bronchospasm.
cards.context:
Bronchiolitis is viral small-airway inflammation with mucus plugging, not bronchospasm.

Treatment is supportive: oxygen below 90% if ≥6 weeks and low-risk, or below 92% if younger/high-risk; NG/IV fluids if feeding is inadequate.

Escalate respiratory support to HFNC, then NIV or intubation if the infant becomes exhausted.

cards.front: Typical puberty duration is 2-5 years; delayed and precocious puberty are defined by [___] (FSH/LH-driven gonadal activation), not adrenarche.
cards.context:
Puberty typically lasts 2-5 years from start to completion. The defining event is gonadarche — gonadal activation by FSH/LH (HPG axis).

Adrenarche (adrenal androgen production) precedes gonadarche and produces pubic hair, axillary hair, acne — but isn't true puberty. Delayed/precocious puberty are defined by gonadarche timing, not adrenarche.

cards.front: A resus adrenaline request must name the [___] — as in 'Adrenaline, 2 mL of 1-in-10,000, IV, stat'.
cards.context:
Volume alone is ambiguous between preparations that differ 10-fold, and a bare ratio is easy to mishear under stress. Naming the concentration inside the request closes both holes.

Do the arithmetic silently, then use one spoken order: drug, volume plus concentration, route, timing. Closed loop: the nurse repeats the request back before giving.

cards.front: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA): arthritis ≥6 weeks, onset <[___] years, exclusion of other causes; most common chronic rheumatic disease in children.
cards.context:
JIA is arthritis ≥6 weeks, onset <16y, other causes excluded. The 6-week threshold separates JIA from post-infectious or transient arthritis — it's the commonest chronic rheumatic disease of childhood.

Subtypes: oligoarticular (≤4 joints, ANA+, uveitis risk), polyarticular (≥5 joints), systemic (Still's: quotidian fever, salmon rash, hepatosplenomegaly).

cards.front: The commonest childhood vasculitis — buttock/leg palpable purpura with tummy pain and joint aches — is IgA vasculitis, still often called [___].
cards.context: The commonest childhood vasculitis. Recognise the triad: palpable purpura over the buttocks and lower legs, colicky abdominal pain, and arthralgia. Watch the kidneys (haematuria/proteinuria).

cards.front: A febrile 7-year-old has focal metaphyseal tibial pain, raised CRP and a normal early X-ray. MRI shows marrow oedema. The most likely pathogen is [___].
cards.context:
Acute haematogenous osteomyelitis in children typically seeds the metaphysis. Early radiographs may be normal, so focal pain, fever and raised inflammatory markers should prompt MRI.

Staphylococcus aureus remains the leading pathogen in an otherwise healthy child; take blood cultures before antibiotics when this will not delay treatment.

cards.front: A child develops puffy eyelids and ankle swelling, with heavy urinary protein loss and low serum albumin. Together these findings define [___].
cards.context: Urinary albumin loss reduces plasma oncotic pressure and favours oedema. The defining pattern is proteinuria with hypoalbuminaemia and swelling.

cards.front: A teenager prescribed amoxicillin for pharyngitis who then develops a florid maculopapular eruption most likely has underlying [___] infection.
cards.context:
A maculopapular eruption can follow amoxicillin during EBV infection. This alone neither establishes nor excludes antibiotic allergy.

Record timing and severity and assess through the paediatric antibiotic-allergy pathway before assigning or removing a lasting allergy label.

cards.front: An infant hydrocele that is larger in the evening and smaller after lying flat overnight is a [___] hydrocele.
cards.context:
An infant hydrocele is usually COMMUNICATING: peritoneal fluid tracking down a processus vaginalis that has not yet closed.

The tell is that it varies — larger at the end of the day or after crying, smaller after a night lying flat.

That is different from the adult non-communicating hydrocele, which is fluid produced and retained within the tunica and does not change with posture.

cards.front: Distinguishing congenital diaphragmatic hernia from cystic adenomatoid malformation on a plain film turns on whether the chest lucencies are [___] with the abdominal gas pattern; in the hernia the abdomen additionally looks gasless.
cards.context:
Both produce cystic lucencies in a hemithorax, and the discriminator is anatomical continuity rather than the cysts themselves.

In a diaphragmatic hernia the lucencies ARE bowel, so they run continuously into the abdominal gas pattern, and the abdomen looks gasless.

 A cystic adenomatoid malformation is lung tissue: the cysts stop at the diaphragm and the abdominal gas pattern is normal. Passing a nasogastric tube settles it when its tip appears in the chest.

cards.front: Under the RCH pathway, empiric early-onset neonatal sepsis without suspected meningitis is treated with IV benzylpenicillin plus [___].
cards.context:
Vertically acquired early-onset disease is dominated by GBS and E. coli; Listeria is uncommon but serious.

Under the named RCH pathway, benzylpenicillin covers GBS and Listeria while gentamicin adds Gram-negative cover when meningitis is not suspected and CSF is normal.
